subtopic: PROVISION OF LEGAL HOLIDAY HONOURING FRENCH SPEAKING CANADIANS
PROVISION OF LEGAL HOLIDAY HONOURING FRENCH SPEAKING CANADIANS
speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. C-139, an act respecting French speaking Canada day.

subtopic: PROVISION OF LEGAL HOLIDAY HONOURING FRENCH SPEAKING CANADIANS
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: PROVISION OF LEGAL HOLIDAY HONOURING FRENCH SPEAKING CANADIANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, everyone agrees that Canadianism cannot be defined other than on the basis of the two great linguistic communities, one English speaking, the other French speaking. Since the French fact is not the perquisite of Quebec, it must be considered as part and parcel of the Canadian reality.
Our centennial year could be the most appropriate time to assure the statutory recognition of a day designed to celebrate the French fact in the whole Canadian territory.
If Victoria day, in the celebration of which French speaking Canadians like to participate, may be considered in some respects, as the English speaking Canada day, June 24 could be known as the French speaking Canada day. That is the purpose of this bill.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not think the situation is exactly as described by my right hon. friend. Expo will open on July 3 at the normal time. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in view of the repeated warnings this week by members of the Canadian Medical Association in Montreal that Canada, right now, is facing a serious shortage of medical manpower, can the Minister of National Health and Welfare say whether he is seriously considering announcing in the near future further government measures to deal with the situation?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare; Minister of Amateur Sport; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the problem of medical manpower in Canada is complicated, as is evident from the discussions that are taking place in Montreal. It relates to actions and attitudes that are even beyond the scope of the federal government.
We have taken steps to increase the training facilities for medical personnel and we expect that within the next few years, as a result of this action, there will be a 20 per cent or 25 per cent increase in the output of medical graduates in Canada. Hon. Paul Hellyer (Minister of National
Defence): Mr. Chairman, in presenting the departmental estimates for 1967-68 I would first like to pay tribute to my able associate minister who has, since he assumed his portfolio, worked in an untiring, conscientious and extremely capable manner in carrying a large share of the burden in this department. The success we have had in streamlining the organization of the armed forces unquestionably would not have been possible without his very strong contribution.
I would also like to express my thanks to the staffs of the chief of defence staff and the deputy minister. Their drive and enthusiasm in meeting the problems associated with the reorganization has been remarkable and the associate minister and I are extremely grateful for their imaginative and capable approach to their tasks. It is particularly significant that, during the period of the reorganization, there has been no falling off of our operational capability. On the contrary, in practically every field our operational capability has been enhanced.
I would also like to thank the men and women of the forces of all ranks for continuing to give unsurpassed professional service to Canada. I may be accused of bias but, unblushingly, I say that man for man, woman for woman, there are no better military people anywhere in the world and we as a nation should be proud of them.
No statement in support of defence estimates would be complete without a review of our foreign policy commitments, upon which defence planning and, therefore, expenditures must be based.
Because of its prominence at the present time, I would first like to discuss our participation in the United Nations. The policy of
June 22, 1967

successive Canadian governments in support of UN peace keeping is, of course, well known. Canada has provided forces for every peace keeping action since the organization was formed. Since 1949 Canada has supplied a component to the UN military observer group in India and Pakistan. Since 1954 we have been providing observers to the UN truce supervisory organization in Palestine, which has been playing an important role in the current Middle East crisis. It is possible that the United Nations may have to build on this organization to supply a UN presence in the Middle East as a result of recent developments. We are also providing the second largest contingent in the UN force in Cyprus, which continues to make an invaluable contribution to the maintenance of peace and stability, not only on the island but in that particular area of the eastern Mediterranean.
Outside the United Nations, Canadian military personnel continue to participate in the international control commission in Indochina.
While the government regrets the withdrawal of the United Nations emergency force from the Middle East, and the tragic events which have followed that withdrawal, it would be a mistake to jump to the conclusion that peace keeping will never be required in the future.
Demands on the UN to undertake peace keeping operations will, the government believes, continue to be made despite the difficulties which have surrounded the withdrawal of UNEF. While the United Nations will not be able to deal with all the troubled situations which arise in the future, it will remain the only international organization which, in most instances, is acceptable as an impartial outside presence.
It is the government's position that Canada should continue to be prepared to help the UN to carry out its primary task under the charter, namely the maintenance of peace and security, provided we are satisfied that the terms and conditions of peace keeping operations are such as to make this task feasible and are compatible with our foreign policy interests. It is still the government's view that the United Nations still offers the best hope of peaceful intervention in certain situations.
Chapter VII of the UN charter provides that the security council may authorize an enforcement action to maintain or restore international peace as it did in Korea in 1950. It is important, therefore, that Canada be in a position to fulfil its commitments under the
Supply-National Defence charter by having a capability to participate in such an enforcement action, should the government decide to respond to a request for Canadian participation.
I am sure members of the committee would wish to join in paying tribute to the members of the Canadian armed forces who, for so long, as members of UNEF in Egypt, played such an important role in the service of the United Nations and of peace. It was typical of the efficiency of this force and our air transport command that, when word came to leave the area, the force was removed in a remarkably effective manner.
In this regard I would like to emphasize the success-not failure-of our Canadian soldiers and airmen of our force in Gaza. To keep the peace in such an area for more than 10 years was a remarkable achievement for the force which included more than 10,000 Canadian soldiers and airmen who served there since the inception of the operation. They should all be proud of their accomplishment.
The fault is not with the peace keeping force-not at all-it is with the failure to come to grips with the social, economic and political problems that made the peace keeping force necessary in the first place.
In the government's view, a military force is only an umbrella under which men of good will may work to correct the problems that beset mankind. Military force-from peace keeping to nuclear deterrence-is not an end in itself, only a means to an end. If we fail to take advantage of the time and opportunity provided by the military umbrella to build a permanent structure for peace, let us not blame the umbrella if after a decade it begins to spring a few leaks.
The lessons learned from our experience in UN peace keeping operations are many and varied. I would like to list a few of the most important.
First, there is no typical peace keeping operation; no two have been alike. Thus, the ad hoc method of establishing each operation will likely continue.
Second, peace keeping is only the beginning, albeit a vital beginning, to the solution to any international conflict. We must come to grips with the root causes of the hostility or the so-called peace will turn out to be a mirage.
Third, and very important from a practical standpoint, is that the rules governing the peace keeping force must be clearly established at the outset, or soon thereafter.
June 22, 1967

Supply-National Defence
This latter point was brought vividly to light by the Middle East crisis. It is of vital importance that agreed arrangements be worked out in advance of or soon after the establishment of future UN peace keeping operations.
The Canadian government believes in the need for a world body such as the United Nations. It believes that such an organization should participate in keeping the peace; it believes the UN should eventually have permanent peace keeping machinery. We Canadians of all political parties have consistently expressed these convictions and worked ceaselessly toward this goal before and since the UN charter was signed.
But, being practical people as well, we have not closed our eyes to the limitations of UN authority to act. We have not ignored the fact that the superpowers do not always share the same approach to economic and political matters. We have not been oblivious to the fact that injustice and a woeful imbalance in the sharing of the necessities of life breed strife. We are only too much aware that, as yet, most nations of the world are not prepared to allow a world superbody to decide what they feel are their interests.
It was considerations such as these that led the government, in the white paper on defence of 1964, to reject the then popular concept of devoting our forces to UN peace keeping only. Instead we set out to evolve a force with a wide range of capabilities to participate in military activity from contributing to the deterrence of all-out thermonuclear war down through the scale of hostilities to peace keeping.
The purpose of our defence policy is not and never was to create simply a giant peace keeping force. Certainly, some of the wide range of new equipment we are obtaining, such as jeeps, reconnaissance vehicles, helicopters, and communications gear will enhance our ability in peace keeping assignments. Of course, the huge increase in mobility provided by our acquisition of air trucks and support ships will mean that we can get peace keeping forces and their equipment to trouble spots faster. But this gear also increases the effectiveness of our alliance contributions and, clearly, the procurement of fighter-bombers, self-propelled howitzers, armoured personnel carriers, helicopter-destroyers and other such items are not those associated with peace keeping forces alone.

[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
The basis of our approach was then, and remains today, one of practical idealism. It was practical idealism in the face of communist expansion that prompted Canada to take a leading role in the founding of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. The Canadian government continues to believe in the concept of a regional alliance of North Atlantic nations. NATO has succeeded in meeting its objectives of halting the loss of territory to the communist world and creating stability in the European theatre. These have been no mean achievements and the Canadian government believes the maintenance of European stability in an unstable world is as important today as it was when the alliance was formed. Consequently we are continuing to provide military support to the collective strength of the alliance, although we are gradually altering the nature of that support in recognition of the changing character of the threat, the advancing technology of military weaponry and an analysis of the total capability of the alliance.
This year the members of NATO will introduce a new system of planning and reviewing their national military contributions for the alliance. The review will take place in the autumn, when the members will submit plans for the next five years. The results of the autumn review will be submitted to the December ministerial meeting for approval. This new system, the establishment of which Canada has strongly supported, will mesh with our own revised method of planning in five year segments with an annual review.
Thus Canada this fall will be required to inform the alliance of the forces we propose to make available for collective defence. Careful consideration is being given now to this matter, but I can assure the committee that if any changes are made in the nature of our contributions they will be of a slowly evolving, rather than precipitous, nature. That is the responsible course for a member of a group. I should say, however, that there has been no discussion of any changes which would have a bearing on the estimates now before the committee.
Another area of NATO with which Canada is quite obviously concerned is the Canada-United States zone. Quite clearly Canada's security very much depends upon the continuing capability of the United States to deter attack on this continent. Although we may be sure that in her own self-interests the United States would have to repel any attack, however unlikely, upon Canada, it has been
June 22, 1967

the conviction of successive governments in Canada that co-operation in the defence of this continent is warranted not only for reasons of pride and self-respect but also for practical considerations of sovereignty. For these reasons Canadian forces have worked closely with those of the United States in planning for the defence of North America. This co-operation is illustrated but by no means restricted to the NORAD agreement, which encompasses the responsibility for defence against a bomber attack and warning of one from missiles.
The semi-automatic ground environment, with its cobweb of communications systems covering this continent, together with its manual back-up and associated interceptors, remains of value as long as a potential aggressor is able to attack with bombers. Unquestionably, the main burden of the Soviet union's strategic capability now rests on intercontinental ballistic missiles. But the arbitrary dissolution of anti-bomber defences, already installed at considerable expense, would serve only to upgrade the strategic potential of the U.S.S.R.'s long-range bomber force, now generally accepted to be approximately 150 manned bombers capable of reaching the North American heartland on a two-way mission.
In regard to an anti-ballistic missile- known as A.B.M.-defence, I am sure members of the committee are aware of the current debate in the United States about the wisdom of deploying such a system. The costs involved are considerable: approximately $10 billion for a light defence and upward of twice that for a more extensive damage-limiting system. To these initial installation costs would be added sizeable annual maintenance and improvement costs, plus probable additional expenditures for improved manned interceptors, and a shelters program. It is clear that a decision by the United States to deploy an A.B.M. system would involve heavy additional defence expenditures. So far no such decision has been reached although development work continues.
The implications for Canada if the United States does proceed with an A.B.M. system are worthy of serious consideration in this country. As I indicated during the discussion of the Canadian Armed Forces Reorganization Act, I would welcome a debate on this subject in this house.

In the discussion it should be clearly understood that membership in NORAD does not commit either partner to participating in aspects of the defensive system. For instance, Canada has never adopted the NIKE-Hercules system for close-in anti-bomber defence, and other than communications, Canada is not involved in the ballistic missile early warning system or B.M.E.W.S.
Similarly, re-signing of the NORAD agreement would not automatically commit Canada to participate in the A.B.M. program if the United States should decide to proceed. That is a question for each country to decide on the basis of its own national interest. Should the United States decide at a later date to deploy an A.B.M. system I have no doubt, in view of the close co-operation between our two countries, that the United States would

I would now like to discuss the general manpower situation in the forces and some of the changes being made in service conditions for the benefit of our servicemen and women. There has been an upswing in recruiting during the first five months of 1967. By the end of May, a total of 6,443 recruits had enrolled in the three services, an increase of 2,727 over the corresponding period in 1966. For those who prefer percentages, that is an increase of 73 per cent over the intake for the same five month period last year.
Hear, hear.
That figure is meaningless. [DOT] (3:40 p.m.)

The month of May, 1967, was the highest recruiting month since 1962. This improvement in recruiting, coupled with an upward trend in the number of re-engagements, has resulted in an increase in the strength of the forces since the beginning of the year. The total regular forces strength on May 31 was 105,972, an increase of 1,015 over the strength at the end of December, 1966. In addition, there are at all times a number of reserves on full-time duty with the regular force, and if the 271 men and women in this category are included the total number of personnel serving in the regular forces on May 31 this year was 106,243.
Steady progress is being made in our program to amend and revise the rules and regulations governing the employment of the men and women in the armed forces. This program has a twofold purpose. It is greatly improving service conditions by eliminating inequities in promotion and employment opportunities and inconsistencies in personnel policies generally, thereby improving morale and increasing efficiency. At the same time it is streamlining procedures which will gradually reduce the costs of personnel administration.
Let me give the committee a few examples of the steps that have already been taken or will be taken shortly:

DEBATES	June 22, 1967
1.	Administration of all men in the forces is now centralized. In the past there were three different systems with disadvantages in each, such as the decentralization of the selection process to command headquarters level, which limited career and employment opportunities.
2.	A common enrolment policy for officers has been established and a common enrolment policy for men will become effective this summer.
3.	A common policy on commissioning from the ranks has been drawn up which eliminates the inequities in the three existing service policies. The new policy will become effective this summer.
4.	The provision by the forces of matriculation level education to those who wish it, previously only available to navy men, has been expanded to all men in the forces.
5.	A common promotion policy for officers has been drawn up and will be introduced in July. A common promotion policy for men was announced on October 1, 1966, which will standardize promotion opportunities in the forces. However, because the previous single service policies were so vastly divergent, the new policy will be introduced in stages.
Steps are also being taken in the fields of welfare and pay and allowances, all of which make service life more attractive.
1.	A new system for the allocation of married quarters on forces' bases has been introduced which eliminates many of the inconsistencies in the former individual service systems.
2.	Moving allowances granted to personnel moving on transfer from one location to another have been substantially increased to a realistic amount.
3.	The Canadian forces social welfare services have been integrated and their services extended to all formations and units in the forces.
4.	A common leave policy has been introduced for all members of the forces.
I would like to discuss briefly what we are doing in the field of management engineering. From time to time we have been taken to task for what might appear to be an overriding interest in the techniques of good management and efficiency.
For some reason some people appear to feel that there seems to be something slightly inconsistent in the suggestion that military affairs can come under the influence of modern management practices. The fact is, and

this has been adequately demonstrated time and time again, the application of formalized management practices in the conduct of military operations is an absolute necessity at any time, but particularly so when operating under strict budgetary limitations.
The development of a small, well trained group of management engineers at Canadian forces headquarters has resulted in substantial savings in existing military organizations, particularly in the field of manpower, and has provided us with a scientific measure on which to base future organizations or new manpower needs. Specifically this group conducts organization analyses, systems and procedures analyses, method studies, and work measurement studies. It is impossible to accurately gauge all the benefits derived from this work but some idea will be gained from the estimate made by the group for the period from January to May of this year when 25 completed studies involving a direct cost to the forces of approximately $56,000 are forecast to return savings of over $900,000. Another example is found in the study of the maintenance manpower requirements for the Tutor and T-33 aircraft which resulted in a recommended reduction to manpower establishments of approximately 16 per cent. The average manpower savings as a result of our management engineering studies are 12 per cent and we will continue to employ these techniques of good management in the months and years ahead.
On April 1, 1965, the Canadian forces communications system was formed to manage the fixed strategic communications services formerly operated by the three separate services, using separate but parallel staffs.
Under C.F.C.S., the operation and management of the composite system has been completely unified, while the actual physical facilities have been integrated electronically and consolidated physically to the greatest extent possible. Coincident with the formation of the C.F.C.S., a program was undertaken to develop a master plan for the modernization and automation of all D.N.D. strategic communications systems. Because of the magnitude of the task, a team of consultants was hired to undertake the actual detailed studies and to develop a master plan for the new system. The study began in September, 1965, and is scheduled for completion this fall. New facilities to implement the plan will follow.
In the area of leased communications, C.F.C.S. has been able to reduce expenditures from $28 million in the fiscal year 1964-65 to an estimated $21 million for the fiscal year
Supply-National Defence 1967-68, saving of approximately $7 million. The reduction may be partially attributed to the closing of certain bases; however, the greatest portion of this reduction is the result of the elimination of unnecessary facilities and the closer control of contract arrangements which has become possible by vesting this activity in a single specialized staff.
While working toward the automated system, C.F.C.S. has been able to undertake a number of short term consolidations which have yielded improvements in operations together with many worth-while economies. For example, C.F.C.S. inherited personnel totalling 3,307 military and civilian. By organization adjustments, an outright personnel saving of close to 10 per cent has already been realized. The major savings in personnel which automation of the system will provide must await the implementation of the consultant study, but they promise to be sizeable indeed.
Perhaps more important than the economies to be realized is the fact the new automated communications system will give the men and women of our forces the modern communication they need and deserve to carry out their widespread duties.
Last August the chief of defence staff ordered a review of the organization and administration of the reserves, including their tasking, command and control, training and equipment. The recommendations stemming from this review were approved last January, after consultation with the conference of defence associations, and the new plan will become fully effective January 1, 1968. A major feature of the plan is the provision of realistic tasks for the reserves within the framework of their existing organization. Units of the reserves will be linked to those elements of the regular force which they must directly support.
To provide more efficient and centralized command of all reserves, the commanding officer naval divisions, the naval reserves headquarters at Hamilton, will be relocated in Ottawa in September and command and control of naval divisions will be exercised by the director general reserves. Changes will also be made in the command structure for militia and army cadets which is now vested in the deputy chief of reserves at Canadian forces headquarters and exercised through 12 district headquarters. The new structure will divide the country into five regions commanded by regular officers with seven small district headquarters commanded by a militia officer to be known as the district commander,

It became apparent during the review conducted last fall that the role, organzation and re-equipment of the R.C.A.F. auxiliary required a complete re-examination and this re-examination is now being conducted on a priority basis. Members of the reserves are enthusiastic about the opportunities the new plan provides for realistic and meaningful training. Development activities for the services, now operating under a single development vote, will continue to be an important item. The management of these activities, as mentioned last year, by the development and associated research policy group under the chairmanship of the chief of technical services is proving to be an effective system. Periodic review of progress and a thorough examination of all aspects of new projects before they are initiated is providing a more efficient and less time consuming means of controlling the development program. It is planned to support a continuing development activity at an annual level of approximately $20 million.
This will include improvements to existing service equipments, studies leading to new concepts and systems, and participation in development projects with our allies.

To be effective, armed forces must not only have well trained and highly motivated men and women but they must be equipped with modern equipment. The men and women in our Canadian armed forces are well trained and highly motivated, and they are getting modern equipment.

As forecast in the white paper there has been a consistent but modest increase in research funds. With regard to the content of the minister's statement, let me say that it was the type of statement which would in normal circumstances be made before the defence committee where one would have the opportunity of studying the great amount of detail it involves. There is no doubt the minister has covered extensively, if somewhat lightly, a great many aspects of defence, including both defence policy and some of the programming he has in mind this year. There are, of course, issues with which he has not dealt or with which he has dealt only superficially. This may be brought out in the course of questions later, although I must say the program of business we have before us does not give us much chance of going into these estimates as deeply as the committee would wish.
Notwithstanding the fact that we had an extended debate in February, March and April involving the affairs of the department, these estimates are very important inasmuch as they continue the program of the integration of command. Even though Bill No. C-243 has not yet been proclaimed, with the result that none of its provisions is operative at this time, there are some consequences which flow from the passage of that bill. It is not my intention this afternoon to revive the so-called unification debate but there are several questions which naturally flow from the de-sion made at that time.
In the early part of his presentation the minister, somewhat self-consciously, I thought, identified with a particular aspect of our defence role, namely, that of peace keeping. His attitude was, I believe, a defensive one. It was said during the unification debate-this is a view which is shared by many who are completely sincere in their belief

that there has been too much emphasis placed on the future peace keeping role of the Canadian Armed Forces. I will not repeat the remarks I made on December 7 following the minister's introduction of the bill. I thought at that time we were going too far for the good of our forces in committing ourselves to a peace keeping role. Peace keeping is not dependent on a decision by Canada alone. It involves a decision which is taken not even by the United Nations as such but by the members of the United Nations. I said in December, and I think I was right, that peace keeping did not have a high priority in the thinking of far too many members of the
June 22, 1967

United Nations. Today I would say they think even less of it in practical terms.
I doubt that the countries of the Middle East care a fig about peace keeping when it comes to practical matters. The Soviet union certainly does not, and it is one of the jokes of the century so far as France is concerned. They may pay some lip service to it, but that is all. We must regret the fact that the concept of a peace keeping role has suffered in reputation. I do not think India cares very much for it. As we know, India was warned in advance by Nasser that the U.A.R. would request a withdrawal of the United Nations peace keeping force, as was Yugoslavia. And they were very glad to get out. This is why Canada was placed in the invidious position in which she found herself. I realize this is not a United Nations debate, but I must say I think the decision to withdraw the force was highly precipitate and wrong in principle notwithstanding the fact that Israel's continued refusal to accept a peace keeping force on its side of the border had not contributed to improving the situation. But that is history now.
The question is: Is there a role for peace keeping forces? I hesitate to think there is in the foreseeable future. And I believe Canada holds the same opinion. I say this in the light of the reservations our spokesman made in the debate the other day with regard to the decision to continue the existence of the Cyprus force for another six months. Indeed, the Canadian representative finally said there must be an end to this situation because almost three years had gone by since we got ourselves into the Cyprus adventure. In that period there has been no fighting, it is true, but neither has there been any solution of the social and economic problems involved.
I agree with the minister when he says that the conflict in the Middle East did not come about as a result of the failure of the peace keeping force. That is true. It came about as a result of the failure of the countries concerned to solve the social and political problems which exist in the region.

I think one can say further that the presence of peace keeping forces in the Middle East and Cyprus is a soporific. It rather lets people forget the basic problem. There is sort of a feeling that if we keep quiet maybe the problem will go away. This seems to allow the nations concerned to dilly-dally or procrastinate and as a result fail to get down to the hard business of settling the problems. It
Supply-National Defence may be that the pressure of fighting will perhaps force people to get down to the matter of really settling the problems. This, however, is one of the negative aspects of a very successful peace keeping force in that it allows the principals in the quarrel to be lulled into a frame of mind that the settlement of the basic problems need not be undertaken now because of the attitude that no one is fighting. I would not agree with the suggestion which might be made by some that I am arguing that we should let them fight to exhaustion and that this would settle their problems. I do not think so. This, however, is one of the negative aspects we have seen in respect of peace keeping and it is something we should keep in mind in respect of peace keeping in the future. I believe some of my colleagues will be speaking on this matter.
With regard to NATO the minister did give the indication that there would be a five-year program disclosed to the member nations in the fall. We would be interested in knowing what the changes by Canada will be which were hinted at in the minister's remarks. Will these changes be in the field of ships? I rather think so. If it is to be in the field of the brigade as a cohesive unit, one finds difficulty in understanding how one could reduce it as an effective fighting team.
The change could have something to do with the ultimate withdrawal of the air division. I rather expect, however, that it has more to do with ships because we are in trouble with our ships. Nothing the minister said this afternoon can gloss over the problems which exist in respect of manpower in the navy and the fact that some ships are and more may be, undermanned. For instance, where is the crew for the Bonaventure to come from? If the other ships are undermanned, where are these men to come from? Obviously they have been allocated to other duties in the interval. They are not merely standing by. I do not believe it can be done by the simple matter of resorting to mere recruits. I thought the minister's remarks about the reserves were rather touching. I was pleased to note that he did not use terms like "bone lean", "sharp" and "efficient" as he did in the past. The truth of the matter is that there are not 30,000 effective men in the militia. Some of our militia units are run down and their morale is apathetic because of the uncertainty that exists in respect of the future of these wonderful units and of our armed forces. We have noticed recently also that during the troubles in the Middle East, Canada at one time incurred the ill-will of the Egyptians and perhaps, but indirectly, of Israel. It may be that those interventions we are making here and there, even if we go about it quietly, are destroying the role that Canada could play in the world, a peaceful role, that of an arbitrator, a negotiator, to bring about peace. I do not think that we can wage war vigorously while claiming that we want to act as an arbitrator.
One might object that we must prepare to defend ourselves, that our territory could be attacked. I quite agree that a minimum should probably be kept here in case, naturally, we should some day have similar problems. But I wonder, as many other Canadians do, if any country in the world will or would attack us here if we concentrate on playing a peaceful role rather than an aggressive role in the world.
Mr. Chairman, we still have so many unemployed in Canada, so many poor, so many old people, disabled, who receive unrealistic pensions in view of the cost of living, and the cost of education is still so high that too many Canadians cannot afford it, that I wonder if we could not considerably reduce the amounts provided for the defence of Canada or that of distant countries and spend them instead on works of peace which would enrich Canada. Why could they not, for instance, be spent even more to feed the two thirds of humanity which are now dying from hunger and have no ears for words of peace.
I wonder, Mr. Chairman, if Canadians, aware that our deficit this year will range between $740 and $750 million, do not think that we should try to slow down somewhat this upward trend in defence expenditures and reduce the burden which Canadians must bear at a time when the cost of living is higher than ever before.
Mr. Chairman, I repeat that many people who want peace are surprised to see that our defence budget amounts to $1,688 million, while our peace effort, that is the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare represents only $1,273 million.
I wonder whether that is in accordance with the appeals made by the great leaders of the world today, His Holiness the Pope, U Thant and others, who warn us that we are on the brink of a nuclear war which threatens to destroy the human race. I wonder also whether Canada is not the very country that should take the lead in disarmament because
June 22, 1967

it is the one least threatened by war and, in view of its history, orientation and national philosophy, the one best suited to act as arbitrator, negotiator and agent of peace rather than of war.
Again, I ask the question in a constructive spirit. The minister should not take it as criticism of his administration, which I think is excellent so long as he wants to have a modern army and prepare us for defence or war as intensively as he is doing now.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
I wonder, Mr. Chairman, and I repeat this intentionally, whether it would be preferable for us to direct our international policy towards a specialization in arbitration, and in order to obtain or to deserve this role, it would be much better for us to reduce our efforts of our expenditures and mind our business a little more closely. Some may say: Am I my brother's keeper? Well, our business would certainly be served more adequately if we had deserved to be acknowledged, by all belligerent countries, as an absolutely free arbitrator, able to propose peace formulas acceptable to all.
I think that this would probably start among other nations a kind of emulation for peace, at a time when we are threatened by a dreadful war of escalation. I believe that this could help to bar this militarist complex which is so hard to eliminate in the world because the old axiom has been credited too often: If you want peace, prepare for war. And, we are getting ready for war so well that it may burst out at any moment.
Mr. Chairman, I would like to repeat to the minister in the most constructive fashion that the purpose of my comments is not to criticize his administration. I believe that he is doing a good job, so long as he is convinced that the general policy of Canada must follow this pattern, but I submit that he should point out to his colleagues that it might be advisable to answer the call of the great leaders I mentioned before, and to prove to all countries in the world, in a very concrete and radical manner, that Canada wants to play a role of peace, and not war, in the world.
I also believe, Mr. Chairman, that when we are faced by the threat of nuclear war, which brings confirmed Apocalyptic visions to our minds, because television shows us once in a while pictures of crowds being burned by napalm bombs or villages being destroyed by high accuracy weapons, with power of destruction unimagined until now, I say that we must cry out in pressing warning and heed it,
Supply-National Defence but not with the mentality of the partisan, set on defending his own administration or condemning his neighbour's. I say that we have to consider this, Mr. Chairman, in the light of our duty towards mankind, as dictated to us by our conscience as men and as Christians.
It is true that we are our brothers' keepers, but not in the sense that we must help to kill them. We know that if two thirds of mankind are now in the throes of such upheavals and conflicts, it is mainly because they are underfed and under-gifted countries, which are denied that reasonable minimum of affluence that we, ourselves, enjoy. We would probably be much more welcome if we helped them still more generously to acquire that reasonable minimum of affluence. At least, they would learn to like us, to trust us, to place their confidence in us, when they have troubles with their neighbours.
I see few countries, Mr. Chairman, in a better position than Canada to assume that role for peace in the world.
I make those remarks to the hon. minister in the spirit in which I presented them to him. I would not be surprised if the minister-it must happen to him at times-were sometime to examine his conscience, calmly, at home, the Holy Ghost might prompt him to discuss the matter with his colleagues. In a few years, the cabinet might lead us toward the role of pacifier, mediator, negotiator, rather than that of the aggressor which we play indirectly at the cost of losing the trust of one third of the peoples of the world.

Mr. Chairman, just a few days ago during private members' hour the hon. member for St. John's East praised executive assistants and said how important they were to the operations of the House of Commons. He said they could be and are helpful not only to the ministers to whose offices they are attached but also to members of parliament. The idea of executive assistants being helpful to members of parliament generally took me by surprise. As a result I got in touch with an executive assistant attached to the Department of National Defence. His name is well known in some circles. I asked him to give me some ideas for the debate today on these estimates. He very promptly replied and provided me with a one-page speech which would not take two minutes to deliver. I did not think that by using that speech I would really be doing justice to the Minister of National Defence
June 22, 1967

Supply-National Defence who I am sure expects members of the opposition to pay more attention to the estimates of his department. I tried reading it out loud to see how it would sound, but the effusive complimentary adjectives choked in my throat. So I had to lay it aside and it is with regret that I cannot make use of the help of that executive assistant who is perhaps of greater help to the minister, or perhaps the minister may think he is, but I sometimes wonder.
On this occasion I will have to rely on my own thoughts and phraseology, which are of course at a lower level, in an attempt to deal with the subject matter before us. I always welcome the opportunity of dealing with the estimates of the Department of National Defence. The minister has told me many times that my knowledge of military matters is primitive, but I am trying to learn as the years go by. Consequently I pay very close attention to what the minister says and to the policies he enunciates.
Today the minister proved a point we have been making over the last two or three years. We have been saying that the policy of national defence has been altered and changed to a very considerable degree and that the main emphasis in the reorganization the minister has undertaken has been on the provision of a force for peace keeping operations. The minister made a statement outside the house denying this and said it is not Canada's policy to produce a giant peace keeping force. The minister asks why we are buying heavy equipment if our whole purpose is to build a peace keeping force. We have never said that is the sole purpose but that the main intent of the government has been to provide a peace keeping force.
The minister proved our point today by starting off immediately to deal with our peace keeping role in the United Nations rather than with our military forces in antisubmarine activities or our activities under NATO or NORAD. That is exactly what we have been suggesting, that what is uppermost in the minister's mind is peace keeping for the United Nations. The construction of his new force is designed for that purpose.
The minister told us that things have changed. Sometimes I like to look back and read some of his speeches, although I am getting a little tired of them. His major document is the white paper and he mentioned it two or three times today somewhat casually during his speech. I knew he would, but that white paper was produced in 1964 and it is


high time it was brought up to date and modernized. Nevertheless, it is his basic document. The second document to which he most often refers is the speech he made on December 7 which was widely circulated at the expense of the taxpayer.
In that speech of December 7 the minister said, as reported in Hansard at page 10831:
The pattern of warfare in which armies fought armies, navies fought navies, and air forces fought air forces is not likely to be repeated.
Only within the last few days we have been reading and listening to accounts of armies fighting armies in Egypt, in Jordan and on the border between Syria and Israel. It is only within the last few days that we read and heard about air forces fighting. It was in April of this year that the Israeli air force claimed to have downed five Syrian planes in combat. It is only recently that we heard about the destruction of Egyptian aircraft in the air and on the ground by the Israeli air force. So the pattern of warfare does not seem to have changed to fit the minister's idea of what modern warfare should be.
The conflict in Viet Nam has been going on now for several years and there has been some activity in the air. The ground forces seem to me to be fighting as ground forces have always fought since the beginning of time. There have been no recent naval engagements. Only two days ago there was a conflict in Aden with infantrymen fighting infantrymen, and rather heavy casualties were suffered.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
The minister tells us that the pattern of warfare has changed and therefore he has carried out this great reorganization. I have wondered for a number of years what was behind all this, why it was undertaken. I refer to our foreign policy and to the Prime Minister's idea of what should be done with Canada's defence forces. As the minister in his opening remarks dealt with foreign policy it is quite competent for me to discuss foreign policy in a debate on defence matters. The white paper on defence clearly states on page 5.
The objectives of Canadian defence policy, which cannot be dissociated from foreign policy, are to preserve the peace by supporting collective defence measures to deter military aggression; to support Canadian foreign policy including that arising out of our participation in international organizations, and to provide for the protection and surveillance of our territory, our air space and our coastal waters.
June 22. 1967

One sees there where the minister places the defence of Canada. It is at the bottom of the list. On page 6 of the white paper the minister says:
-there have developed four parallel methods by which the objectives of Canadian defence policy have been pursued. They are:
(a) Collective measures for maintenance of peace and security as embodied in the charter of the United Nations, including the search for balanced and controlled disarmament-
Method (b) has to do with NATO, (c) has to do with NORAD, and (d) with the security and protection of Canada. So it is not unusual that we on this side of the house and the public generally have reached the conclusion that Canada's foreign policy and her defence policy are designed jointly to provide peace keeping forces for the United Nations and the reorganization of our forces has been carried out with that purpose in mind.
It so happens that the collapse of the United Nations emergency force in Egypt has brought down this policy just like a house of cards. It now has to be re-examined. I hope the Secretary of State for External Affairs will be here shortly to examine this matter co-operatively with us in the House of Commons. Perhaps the Prime Minister will revise his opinion with regard to the activities of peace keeping forces. Then the Minister of National Defence will carry out the orders that will be given to him by his superiors.
In my opinion the whole trouble stems from a misconception of what should be Canada's defence policy. I believe Canada's defence policy should be primarily the defence of Canadian territory and Canadian waters. Second, it should be linked to the alliances that we have with the major powers such as we have in NATO, and with the alliance we have with the United States to protect the North American continent. I believe these activities take precedence over our far-flung efforts under the United Nations.
I am not decrying the value of United Nations efforts to promote peace, to maintain peace, to restrict the operations of nations which are about to engage in war and to restrain them when they have engaged in conflict. I am not objecting to that at all. But to my mind this is a subsidiary effort in so far as Canada is concerned. We should not make this the prime objective of our defence efforts.
I propose to indicate the evidence that has been produced and is being developed to show that it is now generally accepted that the
Supply-National Defence major reorganization and alteration of Canada's defence forces was designed for the purpose of promoting United Nations peace keeping efforts. The disaster that has overfallen that peace keeping effort on the borders between Egypt and Israel should now bring about a reappraisal of Canada's defence policy and foreign policy.
The minister cannot effectively deny that public opinion generally considers that this has been the purpose of the efforts of the present government. It goes beyond that. It reaches into the field of establishing neutrality for Canada. I will give the evidence of that shortly. Foreign observers in Canada have reached the conclusion that Canada's foreign and defence policy is now aimed at (1) emphasizing peace keeping operations, and (2) a position of neutrality for Canada. It is high time parliament had a second look at this policy and passed an opinion on what the government is doing. It is high time the Canadian people were fully informed as to what this government is aiming at. It is high time that in our relations with our closest neighbour and strongest ally, the United States, we made it abundantly clear that we are not adopting a policy of neutrality, that there will be no danger to the United States from an aggressor coming in by the back door through an unprotected Canada.
With those opening remarks, Mr. Chairman, I now call it six o'clock. I will present to the committee at eight o'clock some further thoughts on this matter.

speechtext:
That an order of the house do issue for a copy of any contract entered into concerning taxi service to and from the Ottawa railway station, since January 1, 1966.
[DOT] (6:00 p.m.)
He said: Mr. Speaker, I rise this afternoon to speak on the motion for the production of a copy of the contract entered into between the Ottawa railway station and the monopoly taxi concession which has been granted from that point to the city of Ottawa. I moved this motion in the House of Commons in the ordinary way some time ago and on June 7, as reported in Hansard, page 1253, secured this answer from the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill):
There is no such contract in the possession of the government. Therefore I would hope the hon. member would be willing to drop the motion.
Such an answer begs the question. I simply ask for a copy of any contract entered into concerning taxi service to and from the Ottawa railway station, since January 1, 1966. I did not expect that the government would have the contract in its possession, but a copy of the contract could surely be secured from the Canadian National Railways, which is a crown corporation, if they do not want to call themselves a branch of the government. We were told the following, as recorded on page 532 of the 1964 report of the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, by Mr. MacDougall, the solicitor general of the C.N.R., when he was speaking about the Ottawa terminal railway bill:
The Canadian National Railway will be half owner of the Ottawa Terminal Railway Company, and it will be open to parliament to inquire through the Canadian National Railway about anything respecting the terminal.
I inquired about the possibility of securing a copy of the contract and I directed my inquiry to the Minister of Transport.

I have already spoken on the question of the monopoly contracts which are granted from time to time either by the government or by some department of the government or crown corporation, and this is done by a political party which makes a great show of being in favour of free competition and of letting the best man secure the best possible price in open competition. We say we are against monopolies, we are against restraint of trade and against combines. We make the finest speeches along that line of any political party in Canada. Unfortunately I cannot hear the speeches because of the noise made by the actions that are carried out by various departments of the government or by crown corporations.
As I mentioned before, on March 27 the Minister of Transport issued a press release in which it was stated that the Department of Transport was giving Canadian Pacific Airlines authority to fly more aircraft in Canada during Expo. In that press release, issued under the authority of the Minister of Transport, there is a reference I should like to quote. It reads as follows:
A well known British aviation consultant, Mr. Stephen Wheatcroft, who had been employed by the previous government to report on this matter, was asked to make a further report. His report received last year, indicated that the service by C.P.A. on the domestic-transoonltinental route Vancouver-Winnipeg-Montreal-Toronto, limited to a once daily round trip, while it had not shown any indication of producing either major improvements in efficiency or new traffic, had led to a wider public satisfaction as a result of the availability of choice between two carriers.
If we are going to praise the fact that there was wide public satisfaction as a result of the availability of choice between two air carriers, why do we allow any branch of the government or crown corporation to grant a monopoly which automatically stops any choice between two or more services? In the Ottawa Journal of March 28, the day after the press release of the Department of Transport was issued, there appeared an editorial headed "Freer Enterprise Flight". I will quote the final paragraph of this editorial:
Mr. Pickersgill put it well when he said the main advantage of two air lines was that competition made them both more responsive to a public which felt that a monopoly always was unresponsive. There's nothing so helpful to good service as a choice in air lines, railways or bootblacks and nothing so depressing to free enterprise as a government attitude that monopolies are simplest and best.
I draw this to the attention of the house for the simple reason that I do not believe these
June 22, 1967

monopolies should be allowed to exist. When speaking on the estimates of the Department of Transport on May 26 I referred to this situation and described the conditions as I found them at the Ottawa station.
I believe sincerely that the Minister of Transport is inclined to agree with my contention because I was present in this house on May 29 when he was speaking on his estimates. As reported on pages 708 and 709 of Hansard, he listed the great problems which face the Department of Transport, and there are great problems facing that department. I think it must be the heaviest portfolio in the entire cabinet. I cannot think of any other department that ranks with it for the magnitude and number of problems which the minister must be considering 24 hours a day.

Then there is a reply from Mr. Macdougall, who was representing Canadian National Railways on the Ottawa Terminal Company bill. Mr. Macdougall said:
Mr. Chairman, perhaps I could say a word on Mr. Cantin's amendment. The bill as drafted before you is in the same general form that has been used in bills of this kind before, notably the Toronto Terminal Company bill, to provide the power, but the Ottawa Transportation Commission made representations to the companies and to the government, because they have an exclusive franchise for handling passengers in and about the city of
June 22, 1967

Taxi Service at Ottawa Railway Station
Ottawa which was given to them by parliament. These powers would transgress upon the exclusive franchise of the Ottawa Transportation Commission. We have no desire to do that, or to get in any conflict of that kind. We quite gladly agree that the reference to passengers should be removed so that there could not be any idea that there was a conflict. That is the purpose of the amendment.
Mr. Macdougall referred to the exclusive right of the Ottawa Transportation Commission to carry passengers to and from the Ottawa station. The bill died in the mists of time in the halls of this building, and certainly did not come back to the floor of the House of Commons.
What do we find today, Mr. Speaker? The new Ottawa station is evidently being administered jointly by the C.P.R. and the C.N.R. We have an exclusive taxi franchise granted to one company in the city of Ottawa. We have had numerous reports from members of the house about having to wait for taxi service from the station whenever there is a big holiday crowd or week end crowd returning to the city.
The Ottawa Journal for March 16 of this year referred to the situation in an editorial entitled "Taxis At The Station". The editorial went on to say:
The Ottawa Police Commission.. .Is aware of a taxi shortage, particularly at the new Union Station.
But 50-or even 100-extra cabs spread over the taxi companies of the city will not be the answer to the problem at the station where the taxi franchise is held by one company...
There have been good reasons for complaints...
But some new arrangements are called for to end the frustrating experience so many have had of waiting 30 minutes before a taxi was available.
I can quote to you, Mr. Speaker, fine-sounding statements made by members of the Liberal party to the effect that they believe in free competition, that they are against restraint of trade, that they are against monopolies. I have in my hand Hansard for December 27, 1951. As reported at page 2400 hon. Mr. Croll, the then hon. member for Spadina, now a distinguished member of the other house, speaking about the legislation regarding resale price maintenance, said:
I welcome this legislation because it is in the best Liberal tradition. Historically and traditionally we have been opposed to trusts, cartels and combines.
You could not make a better speech, Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Liberal party declaring how it supports free enterprise than that made by Hon. David Croll. As I said before, I can hardly hear the words for the actions of departments of government or crown corporations.

The other day I had occasion to refer to the comments of Hon. Lionel Chevrier as they are reported at page 2441 of Hansard for December 28, 1951, when he was a member of the cabinet and was fulsome in praise of competition and the benefits that it would bring to the people of Canada as a whole. Hon. Lionel Chevrier had this to say in pointing out how the Liberal government was going to smash the maintenance of prices:
Hon. members will recall first of all that the royal commission on prices under the chairmanship of Professor Clifford Curtis of Queen's University was -and I quote his remarks-"impressed by the degree to which individual manufacturers fix the sale prices of their products, and so narrow the area in which price competition amongst wholesalers and retailers is operative."
I can only make the comment, Mr. Speaker, that there can be very little competition among taxi companies when only one company is granted the right to run a taxi service to and from a station or airport. Then Mr. Chevrier went on to point out that there had been some criticism of the report on the ground that the committee did not obtain sufficient factual evidence. He was referring to the report of the committee which conducted the resale price maintenance investigation. However, Mr. Chevrier said that he did not pay much attention to that because he felt that the committee had secured all the factual evidence that it required.
Last Friday in this house the Registrar General Mr. Turner also made quite a few statements about the benefits of competition and how his new department was going to smash monopolies. One of his more interesting comments is to be found at page 1608 of Hansard and reads as follows:
If I were to suggest something which perhaps Is un-Canadian, I might say I think we should have facts before we have policy.
This, of course, is in contradiction of Mr. Chevrier's statement in 1951 that they did not need to have any more facts at that time; they decided they had all the information they required. I congratulate the Registrar General on being un-Canadian, as he says he might be in getting facts before policy is set down by his department.
I might say, Mr. Speaker, that I enjoyed listening to the remarks of the Registrar General last Friday because he speaks well. I only wish that the cabinet meant what he says as much as the Registrar General says it does. I should like to put on record some
June 22, 1967	COMMONS
extracts from his speech of last Friday. He went on to say:
On the supply side the whole field ot competition must be looked Into...It relates also, on the supply side, to the methods which would enhance the validity of the consumer's choice.
What choice is there, Mr. Speaker, when you have a monopoly situation? He went on:
-so that there are competitive forces at play-
That is a good phrase too.
Prices depend on competitive forces. We hope to ensure that the forces are truly competitive.
What competition is there in view of these airport franchises at Dorval, Malton, Halifax, Vancouver and Winnipeg?
Then, really getting down to the facts of the matter, the Registrar General had this to say, and in this respect I do not believe he was speaking for the cabinet because their actions contradict this statement:
We do not intend to tell the worker where to work-
Yet we passed the railway operations act last September which told the strikers where they had to work.
-and we do not intend to tell the consumer what to buy. We believe in a free market economy. I feel that we should release the competitive forces. This means we must attack monopolies.
I do not believe, Mr. Speaker, that anybody has ever heard finer and louder words, certainly more fulsome words, than those uttered by speakers for the Liberal party on this subject. Yet what goes on? We grant monopolies here and we grant monopolies there. I only ask that the taxi companies of Ottawa, who would like to get in on the lucrative trade out of the Ottawa station, be allowed to see a copy of the contract which exists between the company-I do not know how to refer to it now because the company was not incorporated as a separate company as the bill died. This station must now be run cooperatively by the C.N.R. and the C.P.R. In any event, I contend they should be allowed to see the contract that exists in connection with exclusive taxi service from the Ottawa railway station to the city of Ottawa.
I believe that if this contract were produced it would open up the entire field of monopolistic practise in all airports in Canada. As a Liberal I am very sorry to see the cabinet indulging in monopolistic practice and, what is worse, being prepared to defend their action while placing value on competition to keep down prices and on the free play of the market to make it possible for people to get 100 cents on the dollar.

That, sir, is clear evidence that the policy of this government throughout 1964, and from then on, has been to put the main emphasis on a peace keeping force for the United Nations. I suggest to you, as I did earlier before the supper recess, that it should not take precedence over Canada's own defence, over Canada's commitments to NATO and to our allies in that area, nor over our commitments to NORAD. What I object to is the transformation which has occurred and the emphasis Which has been put on the United Nations peace keeping force while other factors have been relegated to an inferior position. I think we do not thoroughly understand the nature of peace keeping. I reject entirely the minister's statement about the use of our forces, and I quote from page 14431 of Hansard:
...to participate in any action anywhere in the world which might be in the interests of Canada in so far as putting out, containing or controlling incidents which under other circumstances might escalate into something more serious.
June 22, 1967

You engage in war when you try to prevent an armed conflict from escalating into something more serious. Had we had heavily armed forces on the Egyptian and Israeli border and had they remained there, they would have engaged in fighting. Why do we not go to the support of the British in Aden to prevent that conflict from escalating into a major war? What about the situation developing in Nigeria where, we are told by newspaper reports, civil war may break out? What about the situation in Mozambique which the Toronto Star of Thursday, June 22, calls "a forgotten war" where the Portuguese are fighting against rebel forces in that country supplied, as reported, with money and arms from Tanzania and Zambia. This morning we discovered in the external affairs committee that Canada is providing military guidance to Tanzania. Is this the way our foreign aid is used? This is an interesting question which we might ask officials in the external affairs department. Do we really understand the nature of peace keeping operations?
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
I think everyone should read the book called, "Soldiering for Peace" by General Carl von Horn, published in England in 1966, and in the United States in 1967. This man spent six years as head of the truce or observer forces in Israel on the border between Israel, Jordan and Syria. He also spent some time in the Congo, then returned again to Israel and was posted to Yemen where there has been an abortive exercise by the United Nations. This book by an experienced military commander of United Nations forces will give people an idea of the difficulties involved in peace keeping, which it seems to me we rather lightly talk about. There is one sentence in the book in which he says that peace in our times is a bloody business, and it should be so recognized. We are being bemused and confused by talking about peace keeping and peace restoring; we are organizing our forces in an incorrect way, I think, and placing the emphasis in the wrong place.
Even in the observer corps that has been working for years on the border between Israel and Lebanon and Syria a valuable Canadian life was sacrificed, the life of Colonel Flint of the Princess Patricia's, who in 1958 was examining an incident which had oc-cured between the Israelis and the Syrians.

Mr. Chairman, I thank the committee with a certain element of surprise, and I am very grateful. I was saying that one valuable Canadian life was lost. We must ask ourselves whether this is the type of work that Canadian soldiers should be asked to do under present circumstances. General von Horn points out the difficulties of the various missions on which he served in those countries in the Middle East. He tells an extraordinary story of courage and endurance and of coping with untold difficulties. He has praise for various Canadians who served with him in those areas, but he clearly shows how those observer corps forces and the other armed forces that he commanded in the Congo, in Yemen and so on, were handicapped by the ineptness of the administrative services of the United Nations.
I think that our government is thoroughly familiar with the need for a better type or organization in the United Nations in order to put these groups or armed forces in the field. Surely this is partly what the Prime Minister was writing about in Maclean's magazine on May 2, 1964, the necessity for some type of superior military and administrative organization in order to assist in these operations abroad.
However, Mr. Chairman, I very much question whether we in this house have sufficient information about some of these activities. We have been taking it a little for granted, and a book such as the one I have mentioned sets out very starkly and clearly that it is not a simple matter to post observer corps along the borders of countries who adopt a belligerent attitude to one another. It is not an easy matter to post these forces in extremely difficult terrain. It is a very difficult matter indeed to operate and command forces gathered together from various countries around the world, each with its own ideology. There is nothing easy about that at all.
Before we commit ourselves to any more adventures, Mr. Chairman, I think we should re-examine and reappraise the nature of our obligations. We want the United Nations of course to survive as a useful force in the world, but let us not bemuse ourselves by talking about peace keeping missions and pretending that these are going to be successful or will be the answer to the problem. Recent events have clearly shown that the United
June 22, 1967

Supply-National Defence Nations emergency force in the Gaza strip and elsewhere was ineffective in preventing the outbreak of war. I think it is a careless use of language to say that this force preserved the peace for ten years. Peace was preserved for ten years only because the antagonists were not ready to fight. Had they been ready earlier, that peace force would have been sent home, as it was.
The observer corps activities on the border of Jordan and Syria have been relatively ineffective over all these years. This book by General von Horn is replete with examples of incidents caused by both sides, and war was not prevented. Accusations were made, reports were sent to the United Nations. He states that in the United Nations, either in the security council or in the assembly, on 400 occasions there appeared on the agenda a resolution or a reference to the trouble between Israel and the Arab states. So, the political solution has escaped the nations of the world all these years, despite the observer corps on the border and despite the emergency force in the Gaza strip.
What I dislike is the unintentional pretence that these forces really are effective. I think we should reach the conclusion that they are not and that something better has to be devised. Even when war broke out just two weeks ago, sir, immediately the cry was that it was up to the four major powers, or certainly up to the United States and Russia, to prevent the war escalating.
This is w'hat happened in 1956 at the time of the Suez crisis. It was not the interposition of the hastily assembled emergency force that prevented that war from spreading or continuing: it was the pressure brought to bear upon the combatants by the major powers in the world.
Canada played an important part in setting up that original emergency force. The Prime Minister has never claimed that the idea originated with him. His sycophants have repeatedly written and told us that this was his idea, though he has never claimed it for himself. The idea was not new to the world. There was a peace force established under the League of Nations when the plebiscite was held in the Saar Valley. Many people suggested some sort of force be made available to the United Nations to restrict belligerence, and even at the time of the Suez crisis the hint or suggestion that there should be an international force established there was first made by Sir Anthony Eden in the British House of Commons. The message was relayed to Canada. It was considered by the cabinet in 
Canada several hours later, and subsequently Canada was able to propose, and have carried, at the United Nations a resolution to establish such a force. Canada was also very active in getting the force set up.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
This is a good record but it did not solve the problem. I suggest, therefore, that a reassessment of our defence policy is required. It is quite wrong, under present circumstances, to put our main emphasis on the so-called mobile force which is to be available for service anywhere in the world, and to pretend to our people that this force will be able to contain or prevent escalation when trouble has broken out. It can do no such thing. If this force becomes involved, it will have to fight; and if it fights Canadian officers and men will be killed, just as British officers and men are now being killed in Aden. We must be realistic about this. That is why I maintain that until the nations of the world in the United Nations can devise a more effective method of solving some of these problems on the political level, and until they can devise a more effective method to provide for the command and administration of forces that are used under United Nations' auspices, we should pause and consider where our interests really lie. That is why I said before the supper adjournment that the defence of Canada comes first, our NATO alliance second, our NORAD alliance third, and the United Nations' efforts fourth.
We alone cannot be the peacekeeper of the world; we are not equipped for that. We have not the population nor the forces, and we are fooling our people when we pretend that we are ready to take on these jobs when we are not ready to take them on. No government will commit Canadian servicemen to these difficult operations and dangerous missions unless there is some hope of achieving the objective in mind.
Our interests of course are for world peace; but we have no specific interest in some of the areas where trouble is occurring. In conjunction with our allies, we should be prepared to assist, naturally. But what are we doing? We are not assisting Britain in Aden; we are not interested in Portuguese East Africa, we are not much interested in what is going on in Nigeria, and if we were we should not take part in anything in that region. We were not able to take part in the trouble between Israel and the Arab states despite all the talk about our mobile forces being ready
June 22. 19S7

to go anywhere, at any time, on sudden notice. We are not participating in the war in South Viet Nam, yet we are talking about providing peacekeeping and peace restoring forces. This, sir, is wrong.
With the prevailing world situation we should be closely allied with the two countries beside which we fought and stood in two world wars. If there is a third world war those are the countries we ought to associate with-Britain and the United States. The organization of our defence forces should be so drawn that we can co-operate with those great countries. That is where our main interest lies.
Our obligation is to the people of Canada, to the protection of their lives and to the defence of this country. Those obligations can best be fulfilled through our close association with the United States and the United Kingdom. I deplore this transformation of Canada's defence policy, as the chief of the general staff has called it. I deplore this confusing and nebulous emphasis on peace keeping and peace restoring. Those are meaningless terms when one examines some of the difficulties which are involved. General von Horn, in his book which is based on practical experience, shows what is to be done. To commit Canadian servicemen to these expeditions under an ineffective administration and control system in the United Nations would be very foolish indeed.
For that reason, I conclude by saying that I am very dissatisfied with the shift of emphasis in Canada's defence policy. In the light of recent experience in the Middle East I say that that policy should be revised.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre will forgive me if I do not continue the debate, which I have had with him before, about the value of peace keeping. I must say that I read the events of the last few weeks differently from the way he reads them.
That shows the value of debate.

I believe that the fact that war broke out as soon as peace keeping forces were withdrawn does not show that those forces were useless. It shows, rather, that the force is needed permanently, and that it should not have been withdrawn hurriedly. It shows also the necessity of having a better organization to keep the peace. That is the lesson I would draw from the past weeks.
