I suspect that in the world of the future peace keeping forces and the sort of mobile conventional forces that we are now developing will still be needed. If the government's plan is what the hon. member says it is, it will have our support. The future security of Canada and of the world demands that we should continue to play this sort of role. We should play it, not simply in so-called peace keeping operations under the United Nations-of course, we should include those- but we should adopt that role as a major aim of our defence policy.
This evening I wish to deal with a subject which has already been mentioned by the hon. Minister of National Defence. The issue that is facing us in this country-indeed, it faces the whole western alliance in the realm of defence-is of the utmost importance. I refer to the deployment or proposed deployment of antiballistic missile systems commonly known as A.B.M. systems or sometimes as B.M.D. systems.
It is well known to those who have studied this question that crucial decisions face our allies in the United States about future plans in this connection. Before becoming involved, Canada must take the crucial decision whether it intends to follow what is being done in the United States. The decision about the employment of antiballistic missile systems is crucial for the future security of the world and for the maintenance of the type of society and life in which we believe.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
In my view it is necessary that these matters be discussed publicly in parliament and elsewhere so that the decisions, when we come to make them, will be independent Canadian decisions, arrived at in full knowledge of the implications and uninfluenced by pressure. The minister has on a number of occasions given his word in the house and in the defence committee that Canada will not become involved in the deployment of A.B.M. systems until there has been discussion in parliament. I suggested in a question to him earlier in this debate that these matters should be referred to the committee on defence as soon as we reconvene after the recess in order that expert evidence may be called, and the arguments both for and against carefully reviewed before decisions are taken. We have seen in the committee that once a policy decision has been made and the government is committed to it, positions tend to crystallize and the discussion becomes not only partisan but often sterile. When information on these
June 22, 1967

Supply-National Defence questions is made available before rigid policy decisions are taken I believe we are far more likely to arrive at wise decisions. Moreover we would then have the ability to say to the people of Canada that we have arrived at those decisions in the full knowledge of the facts.
Though this is a technical subject, I will endeavour to describe the position of A.B.M. deployment as it is at the present time. As is well known, there are two great powers-the United States and the U.S.S.R. For some time they have been locked in what is called a nuclear stalemate, and this has given to some parts of the world at any rate, a fragile stability. This stalemate has been based on the fact that each of these super powers has so-called strategic or hydrogen bombs in its possession capable of almost unthinkable destruction. These bombs, as is known, can be delivered anywhere in the world by intercontinental ballistic missiles a few minutes after being launched. In addition, this tremendous destructive power has been rendered virtually invulnerable by a variety of means such as "hardening" the missile launching sites or by placing these weapons in submarines which can roam the oceans and pop up anywhere to launch bombs capable of destroying whole cities.
As a result of this invulnerability, even after a surprise attack has been launched the other side would still retain the power to inflict upon its attacker what is called unacceptable damage-a phrase used to describe the power to completely destroy the society in the country which launched the attack and to kill tens of millions of people who would lose their lives almost immediately after such a retaliatory blow.
Because of the invulnerability of this fantastic power, we have experienced what is known as the nuclear stalemate. It is in this context that the deployment of anti-ballistic missile systems is being considered. They are designed, as we know, to destroy incoming rockets, and the proposal to make such installations is under active consideration by both the United States and the U.S.S.R. Three recent developments have forced the United States government, which has hitherto been extremely cool toward the proposal, to reconsider its position. I attended a conference last week at which I acquired a new expression which I should like to reveal to the committee. It is said the situation has now been reached in which the United States has to make a "go-no go" decision. I take it this

jargon means that in a short time they must either proceed or abandon this development.
First of the new factors involved is a technological development which has made it easier to detect decoys in the stratosphere and made it possible, or feasible, at a relatively small cost to detect a great many, if not all, of the incoming missiles and destroy them before they reach their targets. A second factor which has caused this matter to become one of crucial importance to decision makers in the United States is the detonation by the Chinese of various nuclear devices including the hydrogen bomb, as has become known in the last few days. The third is the fact that there has been at least some limited development of an A.B.M. system in the U.S.S.R. for the protection, I gather, of Leningrad and Moscow.
In these circumstances the United States has been forced to consider whether they in turn should deploy these weapons, and since they are reluctant to do so, for reasons I will mention in a few moments, they are now in the process of seeking to make an arrangement or agreement with the U.S.S.R. to forgo or to limit, in any event, these new A.B.M. deployments.
A decision in this respect may be made very shortly but I think the U.S.S.R. has said, quite naturally, to the United States government that if it is to discuss the limitation of A.B.M. deployment it also wishes to discuss the reduction of the immense superiority in strategic weapons now possessed by the United States in the ratio of approximately four to one. The Soviet union argues that it might be interested in restricting the deployment of anti-ballistic missiles systems if the United States would agree to limiting its means of delivery or take serious steps to cut down the immense over-kill capacity of its strategic weapons.
I wish to say something about the financial cost which would be incurred if a development of this type were approved. That of course depends on the type of development. In the language used by those who deal with these matters there could be either a hard point area or urban deployment, designed to defend strategic locations against ballistic missiles or defend cities and larger areas. There are, of course, differences as to the extent to which protection would be made available-posture A and posture B in the terms used by the more technically expert. Whatever system is proceeded with the cost is estimated as between $10 billion and $40 billion in the United States.

[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
I doubt that there are very many observers who do not believe that if this process is embarked on that the higher figure will prove to have been far too low. So, there is a colossal expense of wealth and of human resources and energy which necessarily would be poured into this. This is the first part of the cost which has to be considered. It is not just a dollar cost because it means the transfer of resources which might, for example, be used to deal with the poverty which threatens the world. It might be used to improve the societies in which we live and which certainly need improving.
I have not come to the matter of the Canadian involvement in this matter, but I shall do so in a few minutes. Suppose, however, that the Canadian involvement were to be proportionate. I suppose that would mean the expenditures we would have to envisage would be perhaps a tenth of the United States which would be $1 billion or $4 billion, although I think the higher figure is much more probable and, as the minister pointed out, this involves a continuing expense as well.
The real cost, however, is not just the cost in money or materials which might be involved in this. I should like to read from an article which was originally published in Foreign Affairs by Mr. J. I. Coffey who served in the state and defence departments and on the White House staff, an expert in these matters. He says:
Chief among the costs is likely to be an erosion of the already slim possibility of reaching agreement on further arms-control measures which could promote a more secure world.
I think of that as a very mild way of saying that once you have become involved in this new level of escalation what you are doing is saying goodbye to the very bright prospects of getting an effective non-proliferation agreement. There is an expectation that within a short period a draft non-proliferation agreement will be tabled by the great powers at the Geneva conference on disarmament. But what hope would remain that the great powers would be able to persuade the nonnuclear powers not to acquire nuclear weapons if the nuclear super powers themselves proceed to new heights of nuclear development and exhibit complete lack of control? The hopes of limiting this fantastic nuclear power to the five nations who now have it is likely to go up in smoke.
Those are some of the costs. But if billions and billions of dollars constitute a high cost, 27053-118
Supply-National Defence and if the loss of the prospect for arms control and relaxation of tension is a high cost, is it a cost which ought to be paid for our security or is it a cost which the United States should pay for the security of the United States? I believe the answer is vary clear. The answer is that you do not buy security in this way. All you do is provoke an equal response by the other side which means that the degree of security you have is certainly no greater than it was before.
I should like to quote the words of secretary of defence McNamara when speaking to the armed services committee on, the 1968 defence budget of the United States. This is what he said:
It is the virtual certainty that the Soviets will act to maintain their deterrent which casts such grave doubts on the advisability of our deploying the Nike-X system for the protection of our cities against the heavy, sophisticated missile attack they could launch in the 1970's, in all probability, all we would accomplish would be to increase greatly both their defence expenditures and ours without any gain in real security to either side.
Mr. Chairman, I ask, if you do not obtain security at this fantastic price which you are called on to pay, why pay the price? I suggest the answer is very obvious. We must not be deceived. The pressure to proceed with this will be extremely strong. Simple arguments are made that if you can knock down incoming bombs or avoid the threat of bombs you save lives. This is far too simple. You do not save lives if the other side at the same time increases its power so that the total ability for destruction remains precisely the same. But this is a good, simple sort of argument to make.
I have no doubt that the group which former president Eisenhower described as the industrial military complex in the United States would not be unhappy about the developments which would involve the expenditure of billions of dollars on new equipment of this sort. So, the pressures will be great. If the Russians should be unwise enough, and I think they would be unwise to proceed to an all-out deployment of a ballistic missile system, then the pressures on the United States to do the same thing no doubt would be very great.
The first point I should like to make is that I wish to urge the minister and this government to employ all the persuasive power they have in putting their weight in the scales against this fateful new development by the United States of America. It may be that they have already done that, but as an ally and neighbour of the United States which cannot
June 22, 1967

Supply-National Dejence help being involved in the developments which affect the people of the whole world, I would urge the government to make the strongest possible representation it has in its power to make on this matter before the decision is made. We certainly have no right to veto the decision if it is an unhappy one from our point of view. However, I believe we can claim the right to give advice, or to be heard at any rate on this issue, before the decision is made.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I should like to turn for a few moments to the Canadian situation. Before I do that I should like to say that one of the proposals which now is being bandied about in the United States is that there should be some sort of a compromise measure which would be a light ballistic missile system costing about $10 billion. This light system would not be effective against any all-out strike from the U.S.S.R. with its sophisticated means of delivery. But the suggestion is made that this light system might be able to meet the supposed threat of a nuclear attack from the People's Republic of China. I want to suggest that if that is the type of system that is to be deployed, this country should have no part in it whatsoever. We do not believe that the Chinese deployment involved any threat to this country or to North America. If it should, then I think the answer was well given by the hon. member for Rosedale, who is the parliamentary secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, in a speech he gave at Scarborough last Saturday. He said that so far as that was concerned, the time that would be taken to deploy an antiballistic missile system is far shorter than the time it would take the Chinese to develop an effective striking power and therefore to go ahead with a system before you know you even have to meet the threat would be a foolish thing to do.
As the hon. member for Rosedale put it, a "wait-and-see" approach would scarcely endanger western security. In talking to some of our friends in the United States, I sometimes think that when they see their security in some way related to a future confrontation with the People's Republic of China-as some of them seem to see it-they are making a very grave error in judgment.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
I think their security and the security of the world depends far more on their ability to seek and obtain some reconciliation with the People's Republic of China which is no real threat to the United States and unlikely at
[Mr. Brewin.i
any time to become one. In any event, I urge upon the government, when and if the deployment of anti-ballistic missiles is undertaken in the United States, which are competent only to meet a threat from China, that they say we are not concerned with meeting this particular threat and stay completely out of this.
However, it will be said, and quite rightly so, that this country is linked closely in the defence of the North American air space through NORAD and through other arrangements with the United States. This will lead to pressure upon us, if the United States decides to deploy this system, to acquire installations from them and to buy city defences. This will become evident, and if the city of Buffalo, for example, were to have what purported to be a protection then one could understand how those who come from the city of Toronto, like the minister and myself, might be under some pressure to obtain for Toronto the same sort of defence the United States had seen fit to provide for Buffalo.
There is no reason to believe that this particular form of defence will provide security. As Mr. McNamara and others have pointed out from time to time, once you move ahead to provide a defence against a threat that exists today then a new development of offensive power takes place almost immediately. There is no one that I know of who seriously suggests that this system of deployment would be really efficient. It might, if ever called into play, conceivably have the result of minimizing the loss of life. Again, let me ask what would be the expense and how effective would it be in minimizing the loss of life if the enemy increased his offensive power to correspond.
I suggest this creates a further involvement of Canada in an unnecessary nuclear role. I suggest we cannot possibly afford it, and attached to it is a very unpleasant rider. An A.B.M. system implies the installation of a system of shelters against fallout which in turn involves not only large sums of money out of the taxpayer's pocket or the individual property owner's purse, but a degree of regimentation if it were to be taken seriously at all and not merely as a bluff.
I think the time has come for this country, looking at this independently and from its own point of view, to say that if the people in the United States believe they can afford the billions of dollars that would necessarily be involved in a system of defence that certainly
June 22, 1967	COMMONS
would be provocative and would very likely be ineffective, we do not command that type of resources.
We should say that the resources we have will be directed toward something we think is more important and more useful. I do not know that this committee is the right place to quote from hymns, but a line of a hymn comes to my mind which I think is appropriate. It is "Turn back, O man, forsake thy foolish ways."
The adoption of anti-ballistic missile deployment is just another new turning or step on the ladder in the unending process toward a situation where the whole energies of man will be devoted to mutual terror, mutual threats of destruction and mutual futility. I believe that Canadian people will be in a position, quite apart from what the United States may decide to do, to say we must put a stop to this particular process. I do not mean to imply by that, however, that we cannot or should not discuss with the United States mutual defence arrangements, radar screens and other arrangements in respect to which we could be of assistance both to strengthen their security and strengthen the deterrent power of their own strategic forces. I do urge, however, that the government and the minister afford to this house, through the defence committee, at the first opportunity, such information as is available on this vital and urgent subject. There may not be complete information but there is undoubtedly information that will create an atmosphere of understanding of these very grave issues, so that when a decision must be made the government can make the decision, not based upon pressure but based upon Canadian understanding of the issues at stake. If they do that, I believe this will be one of the greatest contributions they could possibly make through defence measures to arms control and to a peaceful world in the future.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I only want to take a few minutes to make some brief remarks. I for one do not believe in long speeches, because one finally realizes, after analysing them individually, that what took half an hour or three quarters of an hour to say could easily have been said in four or five minutes.

Furthermore, what prompts me to take the floor tonight, Mr. Chairman, is that following the statement of the hon. member and press reports, I received, here in Ottawa, several copies of resolutions passed by town councils in the Saguenay-Lake St. John area, congratulating the department for the way the Bagotville base is conducted, congratulating the base personnel for its courtesy, etc., while I received not one letter that might suggest the hon. member for Roberval could have been right. Mr. Chairman, I would like to point out to the house, to those who are somewhat sceptical about bilingualism and Canadian unity that 38 per cent of the servicemen stationed at Bagotville, in the riding of Chicoutimi, are bilingual. I think that this is certainly a fine effort on the part of our two founding races to ensure a better co-operation, a better understanding and to further Canadian unity.
I would like to thank and congratulate the department, especially the minister, for agreeing to send helicopters to the Bagotville base-two have been there for a few months-which are used to search for military personnel as well as civilians. The fact that they are used to search for civilians is looked upon very kindly by the population. Our territory covers a wide area. In the Saguenay-Lake St. John area there are immense forests and numerous streams and often fishermen, hunters, trappers and people engaged in bush operations are in trouble, far from the large centres, and each time we have asked help from the officers stationed at the air force base, we were received very cordially and when possible-and I can tell you that it is 99 times out of 100-we got the help needed.
To conclude, I would like to say that I had the pleasure of seeing the famous show put on for the centennial by the Canadian forces. It is called the Military Tattoo, and it is
[Mr. Langlois (Chicoutimi) .1

known in French as the "carrousel des forces armees du Canada".
I wish to congratulate the minister and the associate minister, who were certainly very closely connected with this show, as well as the whole production team and all the participants. It is remarkable that these members of the armed forces, trained not to put on shows but to serve their country, should be able to get together

and they number 1,000 or perhaps 2,000-and produce such entertainment. Some of them have varied and rather extraordinary talents.
I wish to congratulate them all. These are the remarks I wanted to make tonight, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, as I understand it this will be the only day upon which we will be able to discuss the defence estimates this session. In view of the hour, which leaves only 40 minutes of the parliamentary day, I shall forgo any general remarks that I might otherwise have made and deal briefly with only a few specific matters. The first is the size of the defence budget. This afternoon the minister put on the record a chart or charts which were designed to show that, in terms of the defence dollar, when compared with 1963 to 1964 the cost of defence had gone down, or alternately that if the establishment of 1963 to 1964 had been maintained, the cost would have been very greatly in excess of what it is at the present time.
This was a perhaps ingenious, but I think very blatant, attempt by the minister to try to continue fooling the Canadian people with regard to the cost of defence. During the past three years the minister has consistently tried to persuade the people of this country and the members of the house that he was saving or was going to save enormous sums of money by the unification scheme he was putting into effect, and prior to that the integration scheme he was putting into effect. But the bald fact is, if you look at the estimates you will find that the cost of defence this year has increased by $115,309,000. That is the bald and actual fact. All the squirming, excusing and fiddling around that the minister does will not disguise that fact from the members of this house in particular and the people of Canada as a whole. In other words, all of the minister's much vaunted program for saving money for the Canadian taxpayer resulted in an increase in the cost of defence last year, and this year in a further increase of more than $115 million.
June 22. 1967	COMMONS
In addition, Mr. Chairman, the minister did not point out that in 1963, when he became Minister of National Defence, we had in this country an establishment of military personnel in the neighbourhood of 122,000 officers and men. We now have between 105,000 and
106,000	officers and men. This is a very serious decline in the number of personnel, and at a considerably increased cost. In other words, we are now getting less for our defence dollar than we were in the past. No ingenious attempt to explain away these figures will be accepted.
The next matter on which I should like to speak briefly is that to which the hon. member for Greenwood seemed to devote most of his attention. I refer to the anti-ballistic missile system which is at the moment being considered in the United States and which we may have to consider doing something about in Canada. I believe it is completely unrealistic at the present time to take a hard position against this system without knowing what the facts are and what the necessities of the situation may be. Similarly, I believe it would be very foolish to take a hard position in favour of it. At the present time we are not in a position to assess what risk is involved. An anti-ballistic missile system would be instituted as a survival measure; in other words, a measure to try and ensure the survival of as many people as possible in this country or the United States. Whether the United States goes ahead with an anti-ballistic missile system will depend, in my opinion, on the assessment they make of the risk involved and whether or not the risk involved makes it necessary to put in a system of that kind. Exactly the same considerations must be investigated by us. At the present time to take the position which was taken by the hon. member for Greenwood, that it is completely bad and wrong, is wishful thinking in my view. In other words, we cannot say that there is no risk and therefore we do not need to do anything about it.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
The next point concerns the satellite communication system which is being developed in conjunction with the United States. Can the minister confirm that this is what he said in fact?

There are two systems, one is a trilateral one being developed by Australia, the United States and Canada for the ground forces, and then there is the NATO system.
DEBATES	1857
Supply-National Defence

I think the minister should give us more information in connection with this matter because, as I understand the situation with regard to communication satellites, there is only room for a very limited number of communication satellites if they are to work effectively. If this is to be a purely military communication satellite, it means in effect that it will not be possible to put a civil communication satellite into effective operational use. Therefore, I hope the minister will tell us whether this is to be a combined military-civil communication satellite system or a purely military one, how it will fit in space and what is the number of civil communication satellites.
The minister told us that the Bonaventure our only carrier, would be back in operation this fall. The question that immediately occurred to me is how is it to be manned? I would like the minister to answer this question. Only a few months ago we were informed in the defence committee that of the 20 odd vessels which we still have in commission in Canada there were only 16 actually in operation. In fact, that is what the minister himself told us in giving evidence before the committee. The Bonaventure and some others were being refitted, but a considerable number were tied up at the docks because sufficient crews could not be found to man them. Under these circumstances, and in view of the fact that the increase in the forces has been very small-I will speak about this subject later-how will the Bonaventure be manned? Does this mean that several other destroyers will be taken out of operation in order to provide the crew for her?
The next point which the minister mentioned was the change in the form of the estimates. He spoke with great pride in this connection, and assured the house it would put us in a much better position to deal with these estimates and to understand them. I agree that a breakdown of the expenditures so far as each of the commands is concerned would be of advantage, but the minister has not given us the actual cost of equipment and administration so far as the navy, the army and the air force are concerned. Thus we are unable to compare what the cost will be in this coming year, as shown in the estimates, with what the costs were in previous years. In other words, we are in a much worse position to understand what the actual situation is with regard to defence expenditures than we have been in the past.
This leads me to the next point. I think the minister owes it to the house to give us this
1858	COMMONS
Supply-National Defence breakdown. If we look in the estimates book we will find on page 318 the details with regard to construction or acquisition of buildings and works and major equipment. We are given no breakdown so far as the army, the navy and the air force are concerned. Thus, we are left in the dark concerning equipment matters. I hope that in this year the amount provided for equipment will be spent. In the past three to four years the amount which was provided in the estimates for equipment was never spent. The money which was voted for defence was spent, but a considerable amount which was actually voted for the acquisition of equipment, aircraft, ships, armoured fighting vehicles, guns, ammunition and so on, instead of being spent on these items was spent on general administration, personnel costs and things of that nature. This is what happened, in spite of the fact that the minister said he was going to make great savings in administration costs and was going to devote the money thus saved to the acquisition of new equipment. In actual fact, as I put on the record in the defence committee and I will not put it on the record here but will merely refer to it, the amount spent on equipment by this government in the past four years has been smaller than has been spent by the government of which I was defence minister in any of the years that we were in office. It was also a smaller percentage of the total amount than the money which we devoted to equipment.
In other words, the minister in effect has done the exact opposite of what he has been saying during the past four years he was going to do, namely to save money in administration in personnel and put it into equipment and forces. The amount of money spent on equipment, therefore the amount of new equipment supplied, has been reduced both quantitatively and as a percentage of the total defence budget, and the cost for administration and personnel has constantly gone up.
There are two or three specific matters on which I should like to get some answers. The minister mentioned with great pride that recruiting had improved. He said that we now have in the forces 105,792 people as of May 31. He did not tell us, and this has been the case every time that recruiting and the size of the services has been under discussion, how many people had left the services during that same period. In particular, he did not tell us how many of the 105,000-odd are actually people on terminal leave. The figure at that time was 104,000 to 105,000 people in the
[Mr. Harkness.l
DEBATES	June 22, 1867
armed forces, but 1,500 or more of those were actually out of the services on terminal leave. They were still drawing pay because one of the provisions is that when a man leaves he draws pay for up to six months, depending on how long he has been serving. However, these people were counted as part of the total figure. I have no doubt that around 1,500 or
2,000	would be included in the 105,000-odd. Until we are given the figures for the discharges during the same period for which the minister gave the recruiting figures, in other words the number of people on terminal leave, we will not know what the correct situation is.
I should like to ask next what the situation is with regard to the four new destroyer escorts which are supposed to be provided for the navy. The minister has spoken in the last year and a half to two years about the building program. Whenever he speaks about the equipment which will be supplied to the services he always mentions this subject to try and create the impression that a great deal of equipment is being secured. However, in spite of the length of time that he has been talking about these four new destroyer escorts, up to date nothing definite has been done about them so far as we have been able to determine. I think an order was placed for some of the propulsion equipment, but we would like to know when the first keel is to be laid. When will a start be made on these destroyer escorts? It would probably take in the neighbourhood of three years from the time the keel is laid before one of these vessels can become operational. The minister having scrapped the general purpose frigate program which I introduced in 1963, it means that we are already at least four years behind. From the look of things we will be at least five years late in even starting a ship replacement program, and it will be eight years before any of these naval vessels are delivered.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
The minister mentioned the hydrofoil this afternoon and said that in spite of a fire that had taken place as well as other difficulties that had developed we would still proceed with the project. I should like the minister to give us the cost of this hydrofoil project over the past four years, and what the estimated total cost of the program will be. I also ask the minister when it is expected that the hydrofoil will be able to go into the water and actually undergo trials. I think it would be prophecy of the worst kind to try and prophesy when any of these craft will be in operation. However, I think we should at
June 22, 1967

least be given the details of what the cost has been and what the future of the hydrofoil project is expected to be.
One other matter I should like to ask the minister about, I do not know whether any of my colleagues have raised it or not, is this. There is a considerable amount of wonderment and disquiet in the services, I am led to believe, over the provision in the new defence act that for 60 days after that act is proclaimed members of the forces will be given the chance to retire from the armed services. I think the minister owes it to the members of the armed services, as well as to the members of this committee, to state in exact terms what the situation is in this connection.
I know that there are several other members who wish to say something, Mr. Chairman, and as it is now 25 minutes to ten 1 will conclude my remarks at this point. However, I hope that before the debate is completed the minister will answer some of the questions that have been asked.

Mr. Chairman, the remarks that I want to make tonight will also be brief. I ask the indulgence of the members of the committee if I touch on a number of matters rather than stay with one specific subject as others have done.
My first remarks are phrased in the form of a question to the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra. I simply ask the hon. member, since what he said earlier this evening was so exciting to him and the members of the government, why it was that they sent the navy to sea a few days prior to the provincial election in the province from which I come.
I suggest that if he is guilty of the charge that I level against him, all he has done by what he has said during this discussion of the estimates has been to give further emphasis to the point that has been made, not only by myself and other members in the chamber but by people outside the House of Commons. I refer to the necessity for serious and drastic changes in the armed services voting regulations, changes which would bring about for the armed services of Canada some degree of secrecy for their franchise. What the hon. member is doing when he stands up and recites the voting habits of the members of the armed services is simply indicating to the people of Canada their political affiliations, and I submit this is immoral and is wrong.
Another question I want to raise was touched on by the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra and the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, though they referred to it in different ways. It centres around the
Supply-National Defence question of Canada's neutrality in the eyes of the world today. I had hoped that by the time the defence estimates came before this committee the evidence given to the external affairs committee at their third meeting would have been available to us, because during that meeting there was a rather interesting exchange between the members of the committee and one Mr. Charles Taylor, a very distinguished correspondent of the Toronto Globe and Mail.
I should like to paraphrase what he said in part in response to specific questions about the attitude of countries like mainland China to Canada because he was quite positive in his reply. He indicated to the members of the committee that if the government of mainland China thinks about Canada at all it is either in the context of agriculture or in the context of our being merely spokesmen for and representatives of the western point of view as expressed by the United States.
I suggest that in this world today we are not neutral. I do not see how we can be. I do not think it is going too far to suggest that it is a little immoral to declare that we are. It is wrong to suggest that we can try and impose on the world the idea that we are neutral, because we are not. We adhere to the principles of democracy as espoused and practised by western countries. We believe in peace. In what way are we neutral, Mr. Chairman?
I think it has been suggested that Canada can adopt some quasineutral role which can be expressed to the world in the form of some energetic contribution to peace keeping. If I may paraphrase what the minister said earlier this afternoon in his opening remarks, he said that Canada believes in and works consistently toward permanent peace keeping machinery for the United Nations.
This may be a desirable role, but I think that the vehicle the minister has chosen-that is, the preparation in Canada of that peace keeping machinery which would be used as the lead instrument and for the primary disposal of the United Nations-is perhaps a little grandiose in conception at this particular stage of our history.
I should now like to pass to other matters of concern and develop a little further some of the questions asked of the minister about the Bonaventure.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
I am curious to know where we are to get a crew for the ship. I am more seriously concerned at the moment about other aspects, particularly about some of the details of the

June 22, 1987

Supply-National Defence cost of the half-life overhaul. If there is any misunderstanding, the minister should clarify who made the basic error in the half-life refit. Was the error made as a result of a fault in the specifications? What brought about the doubling of the contract figure? There is an indication that the figure may yet be tripled. Was the department at fault in writing the specifications? Was the fault in the tendering? Are the companies that tendered not qualified to tender for the half-life overhaul of the ship?
The minister has been asked where the crew for the ship will come from. It is interesting to note that in January the Royal Canadian Navy lost 220 members and gained 137; in February it lost 161 and gained 419-that is significant; in March it lost 160 odd and gained 290, and in April it lost 200 and gained 180. The over-all picture, so far as the R.C.N. is concerned, is not an encouraging one for the task of manning the vessel I have mentioned.
I am curious to know what government decision has been reached with respect to the four new destroyer escorts. I have been told on orders of the day that no decision has been given about the lead yard. My information is contrary to that, but the government will make its announcement in due course. I am curious about the savings to be effected under the systems that are contemplated by the government for the construction of two of these ships. It has come to my attention that the second class of yard in this race-and there are only three or four in Canada-will be asked to tender on both ships and not just on one. This is a serious matter and perhaps the government could say whether what is proposed is government policy. The government must always keep in mind that it is necessary for a commercial yard to maintain a balance of trades and skills. No commercial yard must be put into the position of having to abandon lucrative commercial work in order to raise the necessary force to tackle the vessels that the government wants. The minister should also take a moment or two to answer questions along these lines.
We have been told that since the unification bill passed through the mechanics of both houses and their committees, the efficiency of the armed forces has been operationally enhanced. How does one arrive at that conclusion in view of the fact we have lost 4,500 men and gained only 4,900. How efficiency has been enhanced is a miracle, and the minister has some explaining to do there.


During his remarks he read into the record a chart that covered expenditures for the years 1963-64 up to the current estimates for the fiscal year 1967-68. He dealt with the expenditures that were made in the past, inflated those to current prices, and followed his concept through each of the years mentioned. He dealt with the actual expenses for each year and with the expenses for each year at the 1963-64 level.
This was an interesting academic exercise. But the hon. member for Calgary South dealt in committee with an earlier chart that had been prepared by the Department of National Defence. I do not think the people of Canada are particularly interested in academic exercises. Somebody, obviously, spent much time going down a long, straight road; unfortunately, he wound up in the water.
I will not prolong this point, but it is important for the people of Canada to understand what emphasis the department is placing on different expenditures for the current fiscal year 1967-68. As has been mentioned earlier by the co-chairman of the standing committee on national defence, we cannot do that at present. This matter, too, was referred to by the former minister of national defence. The truth of his remarks strikes me as obvious.
From looking at page 319 of the estimates and glancing down at the headings, mobile command, maritime command, and so on we cannot tell what the actual expenditures have been for naval operations, ground military operations or for tactical air operations. There is no way of sorting out the figures; nor can we determine what the Canadian taxpayer is contributing to our forces in Europe.
This morning, in the standing committee on external affairs, we found that items were dealt with that should properly have come under the estimates of the Department of National Defence. I refer to those items which come under section 1, subsection (d), under the heading "Miscellaneous Grants and Payments". During this morning's committeee hearing I found that two items of special interest were noted, namely, defence support assistance to non-NATO countries, $3.5 million, and defence support assistance to Greece and Turkey, $1 million. In section 2, subsection (a) of the same document under the heading "United Nations and its Agencies", we find that the UN emergency force is listed under an assessment of 3.17 per cent, plus a surcharge of 25 per cent; the actual dollar figure is $729,000, and the total is in the order of $5 million.
June 22. 1967

[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
We have no way of knowing how many similar sums are spread around in these estimates. It is almost impossible to tell on the basis of the present form. It may be convenient for the department, and it may be that in time hon. members will become familiar with the system and know which items deserve concentrated attention. On page 318 we find a simple item of $61,196,000 opposite the word "Ships". Does this represent an allocation for the two lead ships in the new destroyer escort program? There is no way of knowing unless the minister can find a few minutes in which to enlighten us. The matter is of great importance to the area from which I come. The reference to armoured fighting vehicles is identifiable. Here is an item, "Aircraft and Engines". How much of this money will be spent on Trackers? How are we to identify the amounts spent on routine maintenance, minor overhauls, major overhauls of engines and airframes? How much will be spent in the maritime command? How can we find out from these estimates whether or not the government intends to replace any of these aircraft? What will happen to maritime air command when the Neptune is phased out in two years. The Argus is already well through its life. What about the Tracker, half of whose life is spent?
We have the estimates for 1967-68 before us but there is no way of determining whether the government has decided on replacements for these aircraft. Maybe this is not important to the people of Canada as a whole. But it is very important to the city of Dartmouth which through the general policy of this government has lost something in excess of a million dollars worth of payroll in the last three months. The mayor and the people of Dartmouth would be interested in knowing whether there is a future for Shearwater. What about the base consolidation program? It is difficult in these estimates to detect savings from the base consolidation program, yet we continue to hear rumours that further consolidations and movements are to be made. The question of Cornwallis has not yet been settled. The question of Shearwater has yet to be settled.
If the government is certain of its position it should make unequivocal statements of its intentions in these matters. These passing remarks must be true of mobile command, infantry brigade, air division, air defence command, air transport command, training command, materiel command and Canadian 27053-119
Supply-National Defence forces headquarters. It is not possible to tell from these estimates exactly where one stands, and in the absence of some explanation it is easy to see why some of us are concerned. It would have been better if these estimates had gone before the committee where they could have been dealt with in detail. This may not be possible for some time. Failure to bring these estimates before the committee may, as the co-chairman of the standing committee on defence suggested, constitute a disservice to the house. Moreover, as the hon. member also suggested, the way in which the estimates are presently set out may not be in accordance with the legal method. Whether this is the case or not, I am not sure it is really relevant. What is relevant is that no one in the opposition can draw any conclusions from these estimates except that a certain amount of money is to be spent in certain general areas. No explanation is given of what appears under the various headings.
There is one final point I should like to deal with, again not in any great depth. I do so in order to place on record the fact that there is continuing concern about it. Again it relates to the remarks the minister made when presenting his estimates. He announced that several new arrangements were to be introduced. The one which primarily concerns me has to do with the allocation of housing. It is all very well to make a broad statement, as he did. Certainly, the time has now come for a reassessment of the system used. But the minister surely has a responsibility to spell out proposals of this kind so that members of the armed forces may not be left in doubt as to what is meant. If this has already been done, I commend the minister for having done so. I suspect, however, that nothing has been done along these lines because recent communications I have had from service personnel indicate a continuing concern about what the government might do.
I see it is ten o'clock and I will so call it, if I may.
Progress reported.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-PROPOSED ELIMINATION OF CERTAIN STOPS IN LOTBINIERE COUNTY, QUE.
CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-PROPOSED ELIMINATION OF CERTAIN STOPS IN LOTBINIERE COUNTY, QUE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am deeply moved in speaking before such a vast crowd as honours me tonight by listening to the particularly important words I intend to say.
This problem concerns mostly the rural areas and is becoming an even greater concern in the wake of certain decisions taken by the C.N.R., which I consider arbitrary.
Far from me the thought of minimizing the immense services this company has rendered to the people of Canada, but it may happen that in some instances administrative decisions are unfortunate. This is the kind of case I should like to bring to the attention of this house tonight and to the attention of the parliamentary secretary of the Minister of Transport, the distinguished member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne) who, to my mind, often shows a marked superiority over his colleague for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge).
Mr. Speaker, the C.N.R. has decided rather suddenly that passenger trains would no longer stop in the picturesque and lively municipality of Manseau, in the constituency of Lotbiniere. One characteristic of Manseau is a very hard-working population.
When speaking of Manseau, I feel I should stress the importance of the achievements of the Savoie family, one of the wonderful French-Canadian famliies, which is a real honour for the people of the Lotbiniere county and which has rendered this whole county, but particularly Manseau, services about which we will never hear enough.
I received recently a copy of a resolution passed by the municipal council of the village of Manseau, whose mayor is Mr. Telesphore Soucy. I also received a copy of a resolution passed by the municipal council of Saint-Joseph de Blandford and the parish of Manseau. The secretary-treasurer of these two municipalities, notary Normand Pro-vencher, wrote to me in somewhat alarming terms precisely to call my attention to this very deplorable situation created by the

elimination of the Canadian National stopover at Manseau.
After having consulted the stationmaster, Mr. Marquis-another prominent citizen who works devotedly for the good of his community-he told me this: "At Manseau, at least $500 worth of tickets are sold each month."
Now, Mr. Speaker, it is understandable in some respects that the C.N.R. would like to eliminate some stops for passenger trains in communities where it sells practically no tickets. But when, on the average, up to $500 worth of tickets are sold each month, I think that the C.N.R. has nothing to lose by stopping for a few moments to let passengers come aboard.
Whenever there are no passengers, the train could go right through. But, today, means of communications are sufficiently developed for the conductor of the train to be advised, some distance away, that a few passengers wish to board the train. Therefore, it would be quite fitting to reverse the decision, which I deplore this evening in this brief debate.
What burns me up most, Mr. Speaker, is the affront to rural areas. I quite understand that urban centres are numerically more important, but I feel that legitimate consideration would be shown our rural areas by keeping the stop system for passenger trains, in order to pick up passengers who live not necessarily in the town I am referring to, namely Manseau, but in neighboring villages. In fact, Mr. Speaker, the parishes of Sainte-Sophie-de-Levrard, Sainte-Cecile-de-Levrard, and Saint-Pierre-les-Becquets are beautiful municipalities which do us honour and which we are happy to have as components of the beautiful territory of the Lotbiniere county.
The people who live in those municipalities, located a few miles away from Manseau, come to Manseau to take the train and go to Drummondville or Montreal. Therefore, this is useful not only for the people of Manseau but also for the surrounding communities.
In view of the somewhat arbitrary and quite sudden decision of the C.N.R., I think that I must share the sad feelings expressed by the mayors of Manseau and Saint-Jean-de-Blandford, by notary Provencher, by the secretary-treasurer of both municipalities, and by the station master, Mr. Marquis, by the Savoie family, in short, by all the others who are interested in the economic development of their area.
June 22, 1967

That is why, Mr. Speaker, with your indulgence, I request that steps be taken to rectify the situation.

maintopic: TELEVISION-NAPANEE, ONT.-REQUEST FOR APPROVAL OF CABLE FACILITIES

speechtext:
Mr. A. D. Alkenbrack (Prince Edward-
Lennox): Mr. Speaker, I bring a matter before the house this evening as a result of a question that I asked the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill), on Tuesday, June 20, regarding a request for approval of cable television facilites in the town of Napanee. My question appears at page 1713 of Hansard. It arises as a result of the application of Mr. Reginald C. Dawson of Napanee who made application to the Department of Transport on February 23 last for authority to establish and operate a commercial T.V. receiving service at Napanee, Ontario. According to a letter 27053-1191
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion dated May 2 written to Mr. Dawson, his application has been rejected. I quote a letter received by Mr. Dawson from Mr. W. A. Caton, controller, radio regulations division of the Department of Transport. This letter, Mr. Speaker, exemplifies nothing but a complete bureaucratic run-around that has been given to my constituent and townsman. The letter reads:
Your application dated February 23, 1967 lor authority to establish and operate a land station performing a commercial broadcasting receiving service at Napanee, Ontario, has been considered in accordance with the announcement made by the Minister of Transport in the House of Commons on July 22, 1964.
The Board of Broadcast Governors believes that the establishment and operation of a C.A.T.V. system at Napanee, Ontario, such as you propose, would inhibit the provision of alternative television service to the area.
Policy problems relating to C.A.T.V. are receiving the attention of the government and it is expected that parliament will have an opportunity to consider this matter in due course possibly on the basis °f amending legislation. In the circumstances, the minister does not propose to approve your application at the present time. This decision on youi application at this time is without prejudice to your right to re-apply once this matter has been dealt with by parliament.
Arrangements are being made to refund the deposit in the amount of $25 which was submitted in support of this application.
Yours truly,
W. A. Caton,
Controller,
Radio Regulations Division.
Mr. Speaker, it is readily apparent that this is an example of bureaucracy at its very worst. What inhibitions are they referring to in that letter? To what alternative television service are they referring? The town of Napanee has about 5,000 people and consists of approximately 2,000 homes. One C.A.T.V. system at Napanee could serve the municipality, and any enterprise that goes to the trouble of obtaining a franchise to instal cable along the streets would no doubt obtain most of the business from the householders who could be served.
Mr. Caton's letter also refers to an announcement made in the house by the Minister of Transport on July 22, 1964. Mr. Caton's rejection of this application simply hides behind the announcement made by the minister long ago, and uses it as a shallow and ill-founded excuse for not granting the application. I am sure the minister does not agree with this, but when we look back to what the minister said on July 22, 1964, we find that his announcement does not apply to this application at all. At that time the minister announced that they simply wanted to

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion make sure that an effective degree of Canadian ownership and control of C.A.T.V. installations was ensured. In the case at Napanee the applicant and his whole enterprise is 100 per cent Canadian. In fact, the announcement of the Minister of Transport on that day almost three years ago proclaims the lifting of the so-called freeze on the granting of C.A.T.V. applications. I quote some of the minister's words which can be found at the bottom of page 5799 of Hansard for that day:
In announcing the lifting of the so-called freeze the government wishes to emphasize that it has no desire to regulate C.A.T.V. for the sake of regulation. but merely to the minimum extent deemed necessary to maintain the Canadian identity and character of broadcasting-
I contend, and I am sure the minister agrees, that a responsible applicaton, such as this one, from a resident of the municipality, especially an urban municipality, where cable facilities are economically and physically feasible, should be quite in order and that the federal Department of Transport has no right to withhold a franchise for these services providing the applicant and user of the services agrees to comply fully with the lighting and marking of his tower or mast so that it does not become a hazard to the rest of the nation by endangering the flight of aircraft.
The mayor of Napanee points out in this letter to the minister that other franchises have been granted in other towns in Ontario, and yet the Napanee franchise is refused for no good reason at all by one of our bureaucrats who uses a speech made by the minister three years ago as an irrelevant excuse for withholding this much needed service from the people of Napanee. I wish to quote the mayor's letter. It reads as follows:
It has come to my attention that one of my citizens Mr. Reginald Dawson has presented an application to your board by which he is seeking to secure a licence or franchise to instal cable T.V. in our town of Napanee.	,
During the last three years we have had several outside groups make contact with our council and public utilities with the idea of supplying us with this type of T.V. service, however nothing has been finalized, and we now have a local group headed by Mr. Dawson who are endeavouring to bring cable T.V. to Napanee. I might add that due to our town being located in a valley, regular T.V. reception is very, very poor and like all other growing municipalities we are anxious to have the best for our citizens.
I note with interest that Smiths Falls, also Belleville in eastern Ontario and Fergus and Elora in western Ontario have been granted a licence to instal cable T.V.

Therefore I sincererly hope that you will give your support to the application that has been presented to your department from citizens of the town of Napanee.
Thank you, I remain.
Yours very truly,
Lome A. Smart,
Mayor of Napanee.
As has been pointed out by the mayor, much of Napanee lies in a hollow between the Roblin Hill escarpment on the east and south and Piety Hill which rises at the west end of the town. The highest land is south of the Napanee River and it precludes good television reception by way of the conventional household aerials.
Many of our townsmen would subscribe to C.A.T.V. when it is available and then many would probably abandon their unsightly aerials. This application should be granted with no further delay.
I am sure the minister agrees that now this franchise should be favourably considered and granted, and I respectfully request him to do so.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I trust I will behave rather differently from the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette) and will stop at the right whistle.
The question of the expropriation by governments or their agencies, both federal and provincial, is of increasing concern to farmers across Canada. So far as 1 am concerned, I can speak for many farmers in my constituency who have suffered from the present law
June 22, 1967	COMMONS
and present procedures with regard to the expropriation of land for highways, for power lines, for gas pipe lines and for other purposes required by the government in question, whether it be federal, provincial or municipal. They have also suffered to a great extent during the last couple of years from expropriations necessary under the terms of the Columbia River treaty.
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
This matter is of increasing concern to farmers across Canada, and on that account a special meeting of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture was held in May to consider all aspects and to study the question carefully. I might say that in no place in Canada, either under federal or under provincial authority, do procedures and principles which are followed in connection with the expropriation of lands and of rights to the use of land give farmers an entirely fair break. It all depends on the government or the agency that is expropriating the property. In some cases there has been little cause for dissatisfaction, but in the majority of cases, in my experience, injustice has been done to many people.
This meeting was called because the overall bargaining position of the farmer is weak compared to the bargaining power of the authority that wishes to take over his property. As a result of this meeting, the following memorandum regarding a solution to the problem was passed which reads as follows:
Experience of those at the meeting, it was noted, indicates that the expropriated property-owner in the city similarly receives less than justice, as often as not.
The solution to the problem, the meeting concluded, must be found in:
Effective united action by affected property-owners in cases of expropriation. Without the strength that comes by uniting together the small property-owner is in a well-nigh hopeless position of weakness.
Improved legislation that will spell out the rights of the property-owner in detail, and provide fair and economical means for ensuring that these rights are realized through adjudication and legal processes.
Improved service to property-owners by their farm organizations and, especially, stepped up programs of information to farmers about their rights under the law.
Then the meeting went on to recommend:
-that in the near future the Canadian Federation of Agriculture follow up its oft-repeated demand for improved federal legislation with detailed legislative proposals to government for consolidation and amendment of present federal legislation dealing with expropriation.
The meeting also discussed some other questions. It was on this account that I asked my question of the Minister of Agriculture on

questions between federal and provincial governments and get, shall I say, some order in dealing with this situation which is of great concern to the farmers all across Canada.
